---
title: "Centering a predictor"
---

In a [simple linear regression](simple-linear-regression.qmd), the intercept is the conditional mean at predictor value zero. Suppose observed surprisal values range from 2 to 9 bits. The intercept in

$$
m(x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x
$$

describes a word with surprisal 0, outside the observed range.

We can make a more useful reference point by [**centering**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=102) the predictor.

Centering is a reparameterization. It changes which predictor value receives the
label zero and thus changes the intercept attached to that label. It does not
change the distances among observations.

## Subtracting a declared reference

Let 5 bits be the reference value and define

$$
X_i^c=X_i-5.
$$

The conversion is

| original surprisal $X$ | centered surprisal $X^c$ |
|---:|---:|
| 2 | $-3$ |
| 5 | $0$ |
| 9 | $4$ |

Zero on the centered scale now represents 5 bits on the original scale.

Negative centered values do not represent negative surprisal. A value of
$x^c=-3$ means three bits below the declared reference, which is 2 bits on the
original scale. Centered values must be interpreted together with the subtracted
reference.

## Rewriting the line

Use

$$
m(x^c)=\beta_0^c+\beta_1^c x^c.
$$

At $x^c=0$,

$$
m(0)=\beta_0^c.
$$

Thus the centered intercept is the expected response at 5 bits.

Substitute $x^c=x-5$ into the centered line:

$$
m(x)=\beta_0^c+\beta_1^c(x-5).
$$

For this to describe the same line as $\beta_0+\beta_1x$, the slope remains

$$
\beta_1^c=\beta_1,
$$

while the intercept becomes

$$
\beta_0^c=\beta_0+5\beta_1.
$$

## Checking that predictions remain unchanged

Let $\beta_0=5.70$ and $\beta_1=.06$. The original prediction at 7 bits is

$$
5.70+.06(7)=6.12.
$$

The centered intercept is

$$
5.70+5(.06)=6.00.
$$

At 7 bits, $x^c=2$, so the centered prediction is

$$
6.00+.06(2)=6.12.
$$

The fitted mean is identical. Centering changes coefficient interpretation, not the line.

We can verify the equality over all three values in the table:

```{r}
#| label: check-centered-predictions
#| echo: true
x <- c(2, 5, 9)
x_centered <- x - 5

beta_0 <- 5.70
beta_1 <- .06
beta_0_centered <- beta_0 + 5 * beta_1

original_prediction <- beta_0 + beta_1 * x
centered_prediction <- beta_0_centered + beta_1 * x_centered

data.frame(
  x = x,
  x_centered = x_centered,
  original_prediction = original_prediction,
  centered_prediction = centered_prediction
)
```

Every row contains the same two predictions. This equality is the diagnostic
for a correct reparameterization.

## Choosing the reference from the question

Several references may be defensible.

1. A theoretical baseline makes the intercept describe a linguistically
   specified predictor value.
2. A conventional value, such as 5 bits, may make the intercept straightforward to interpret.
3. The sample mean makes centered predictor values sum to zero in the observed
   sample.

These choices do not alter the slope in simple linear regression, but they alter
the question answered by the intercept. Centering at 5 bits asks for the
expected response at 5 bits. Centering at the sample mean asks for the expected
response at the average predictor value in that sample.

The sample mean is not automatically the most theoretically useful reference.
If two experiments have different surprisal distributions, their mean-centered
intercepts refer to different original values. A common declared reference can
make comparisons across experiments easier to interpret.

## Distinguishing centering from scaling

Centering subtracts a reference:

$$
x^c=x-a.
$$

Scaling divides by a positive constant:

$$
x^s=\frac{x}{b}.
$$

Centering changes the intercept but preserves a one-unit difference. Scaling
changes what one unit means and thus changes the numerical slope. If surprisal
is divided by 2, a one-unit increase on the new scale corresponds to a two-bit
increase on the old scale.

The two operations can be combined, but they answer different interpretive
needs. A report should state both the subtracted reference and any divisor.

## Reporting the reference value

Centering at the sample mean, a theoretical baseline, and a conventional value produce different intercepts. The analysis must state which value was subtracted.

## Interpreting the centered reference value

An interpretation must not silently treat the centered zero as the original
zero. Suppose $x^c=x-5$ and the
centered intercept is 6.00. An incorrect interpretation would describe 6.00 as the expected response at
zero bits. The correct description is the expected response at 5 bits.

This error can survive a technically correct fit because predictions remain
unchanged. It is an interpretive failure, not an optimization failure. Reporting
the centering constant beside the coefficient prevents it.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the slope"}
1. Why does subtracting 5 from every predictor value preserve every one-unit
   difference between observations?
2. If the original intercept is 4.2 and the slope is .3, what is the intercept
   after centering at 10?
3. What original surprisal does $x^c=-2$ represent when the centering constant is
   5?
4. Explain why mean centering can make intercepts across two samples refer to
   different original predictor values.
:::
